title: Wave phenomena

assemble.prompt: Match each term to its definition.

items.label: Refraction
items.clue: The change in direction of a wave when it crosses a boundary obliquely into a medium in which its speed is different.

items.label: Diffraction
items.clue: The spreading of a wave into the region behind an obstacle, or beyond the edges of an aperture, where a straight-line (ray) model would predict a shadow.

items.label: Destructive interference
items.clue: Superposition of two waves that arrive in antiphase, giving a resultant amplitude equal to the difference of the individual amplitudes, zero if they are equal.

items.label: Wavefront
items.clue: A line (in two dimensions) or surface (in three dimensions) joining neighbouring points of a wave that oscillate in phase, for example all the points on one crest.

questions.stem: Light meets the boundary between two transparent media. Which statement gives a condition that must be met for total internal reflection to occur?

options.text: The light must be travelling towards a medium of higher refractive index.
The light must be travelling towards a medium of lower refractive index.
The ray's angle to the surface must be greater than the critical angle.
The angle of incidence must be equal to the critical angle for the boundary.

questions.explanation: A critical angle exists only when light travels towards a medium of lower refractive index (for example glass to air), because only then can the angle of refraction reach 90°. This is one of the two conditions; the other is that the angle of incidence, measured from the normal, is greater than the critical angle.

questions.stem: A ray of light passes from air into a transparent liquid. The incident ray makes an angle of 40.0° with the surface of the liquid and the refracted ray makes an angle of 55.0° with the surface. The speed of light in air is 3.00 × 10⁸ m s⁻¹. What is the speed of light in the liquid?
questions.explanation: Angles are measured from the normal: θ₁ = 90.0° − 40.0° = 50.0° and θ₂ = 90.0° − 55.0° = 35.0°. From sin θ₂/sin θ₁ = v₂/v₁, v₂ = 3.00 × 10⁸ × sin 35.0°/sin 50.0° = 2.25 × 10⁸ m s⁻¹. The ray bends towards the normal, consistent with slowing down.

questions.stem: Two pulses of the same shape and width travel towards each other along a stretched string. Pulse P has a maximum displacement of +3.0 cm and pulse Q a maximum displacement of −1.0 cm. Which statement about the pulses is correct?

options.text: While the peaks coincide, the maximum displacement of the string is +4.0 cm.
After they have overlapped, the pulses rebound and travel back the way they came.
While their peaks coincide, the string's maximum displacement is +2.0 cm.
After they have overlapped, they stay combined as one pulse of +2.0 cm.

questions.explanation: By the principle of superposition, displacements add with their signs: +3.0 cm + (−1.0 cm) = +2.0 cm. Because the pulses have the same shape, the combined displacement is largest where the peaks meet. Afterwards the pulses pass through each other and each continues with its original shape and direction.

questions.stem: Two identical sodium lamps placed side by side illuminate a white screen. No interference fringes can be seen anywhere on the screen. Which statement explains this?

options.text: The phase difference between the light from the two lamps changes rapidly and randomly, so they are not coherent.
Light waves from two separate lamps cannot superpose, so they pass through each other without interfering.
The lamps have the same frequency, so they are coherent and fringes form, but they are too fine to be seen.
Stable interference fringes can be produced only with laser light, and sodium lamps do not emit laser light.

questions.stem: Two dippers vibrating in phase act as coherent sources S₁ and S₂ on a ripple tank, producing waves of wavelength 2.0 cm. Point P is 31.0 cm from S₁ and 37.0 cm from S₂. What kind of interference occurs at P?

options.text: Destructive: the paths are 15.5λ and 18.5λ, not whole numbers of λ
Destructive: the path difference, 3λ, is an odd number of λ
Neither: maxima occur only where P is equidistant from S₁ and S₂
Constructive: the path difference is 6.0 cm, which is 3λ

questions.explanation: Path difference = 37.0 cm − 31.0 cm = 6.0 cm = 3 × 2.0 cm = 3λ. A whole number of wavelengths means the waves from the in-phase sources arrive in phase, so the interference at P is constructive.

questions.stem: Two loudspeakers connected to the same signal generator emit sound in phase at a frequency of 680 Hz. The speed of sound in air is 340 m s⁻¹. What is the smallest path difference that gives destructive interference?
questions.explanation: λ = v/f = 340/680 = 0.50 m. Destructive interference needs path difference = (n + ½)λ, and the smallest value is for n = 0: ½ × 0.50 m = 0.25 m.

questions.stem: In a Young's double-slit experiment, monochromatic light is incident normally on two slits whose centres are 0.40 mm apart; each slit is 0.030 mm wide. The screen is 1.60 m from the slits. The distance from the centre of the 1st bright fringe to the centre of the 11th bright fringe is 24.0 mm. What is the wavelength of the light?

A ray of light travelling in glass of refractive index 1.50 meets a flat boundary with water of refractive index 1.33. The ray makes an angle of 35.0° with the boundary. What happens to the ray at the boundary?

options.text: It refracts into the water; the angle of refraction is 40.3°
It refracts into the water; the angle of refraction is 46.6°
It is totally internally reflected back into the glass block
It refracts into the water; the angle of refraction is 67.5°

questions.explanation: The angle of incidence is measured from the normal: θ₁ = 90° − 35.0° = 55.0°. The critical angle is given by sin c = 1.33/1.50, so c = 62.5°. Since 55.0° < 62.5°, the ray refracts (with some partial reflection): sin θ₂ = 1.50 × sin 55.0°/1.33 = 0.924, θ₂ = 67.5°, bending away from the normal as it speeds up.

questions.stem: Monochromatic light has a wavelength of 450 nm in water, of refractive index 1.33. The light passes from the water into glass of refractive index 1.50. What is its wavelength in the glass?

options.text: 508 nm
399 nm
450 nm
300 nm

questions.explanation: The frequency is unchanged, so λ₂/λ₁ = v₂/v₁ = n₁/n₂. λ₂ = 450 nm × 1.33/1.50 = 399 nm. The glass has the larger refractive index, so the light is slower and its wavelength shorter there.

questions.stem: Two pulses of identical shape and size but opposite displacement travel towards each other along a stretched string. At one instant they overlap exactly and the whole string is momentarily straight. Which statement about this instant, and what follows it, is correct?

options.text: The pulses have cancelled each other out; the string stays straight from now on.
The string is straight but moving; the pulses then emerge and continue past each other.
The string is straight and at rest; the pulses' energy has become internal energy of the string.
The pulses have collided; each then travels back the way it came, with its shape restored.

questions.stem: In a Young's double-slit experiment using a filament lamp, the light passes through a single narrow slit before it reaches the double slit. What is the purpose of the single slit?

options.text: It makes the light monochromatic, because sources of a single frequency are automatically coherent.
It turns the lamp's light into laser-like light, without which stable fringes cannot be produced.
It lights both slits with the same wavefronts, so the two slits act as coherent sources.
It forms a sharp image of the lamp on the double slit, so that each slit casts a bright image on the screen.

questions.stem: Two loudspeakers, driven in phase by the same signal generator, face a line along which a microphone is moved. Starting from the central maximum of loudness, the microphone is moved along the line to the third maximum away from the centre. At that point its distances from the two speakers differ by 0.60 m. What is the wavelength of the sound?
questions.explanation: For sources in phase, maxima occur where the path difference is nλ, and the central maximum is n = 0. The third maximum from the centre is n = 3, so 3λ = 0.60 m and λ = 0.20 m.

questions.stem: Monochromatic light of wavelength 600 nm is incident normally on a single rectangular slit of width 0.12 mm. A screen is 2.0 m from the slit. What is the width of the central maximum on the screen, measured between the first minima on either side?
questions.explanation: θ = λ/b = (600 × 10⁻⁹)/(0.12 × 10⁻³) = 5.0 × 10⁻³ rad is the angle from the centre to the first minimum on one side. On the screen that is Dθ = 2.0 × 5.0 × 10⁻³ = 1.0 × 10⁻² m, so the full width between the two first minima is 2.0 × 10⁻² m.

questions.stem: Monochromatic light is incident normally on two slits, each of width b, whose centres are a distance d apart, where d is several times b. Which describes the pattern on a distant screen?

options.text: Equally spaced fringes of equal brightness across the whole screen, as in the ideal Young's pattern
Fringes whose spacing is set by the slit width b, within an envelope whose width is set by d alone
Two bright bands, one opposite each slit and each as wide as a slit, with a dark gap between them
Equally spaced fringes whose brightness follows the single-slit pattern, fading at its minima

questions.stem: Light of wavelength 650 nm is incident normally on a diffraction grating that has 600 lines per millimetre. At what angle to the straight-through direction is the second-order maximum observed?

Monochromatic light of wavelength 600 nm is incident normally on a single slit, and the diffraction pattern is viewed on a distant screen. The slit width is then reduced from 0.20 mm to 0.10 mm. How does the central maximum change?

options.text: It becomes half as wide and less intense, as it is an image of a slit that is now half as wide.
It is unchanged, as both slits are far wider than 600 nm, so neither diffracts significantly.
It becomes twice as wide and less intense, as less light passes and is spread over a wider angle.
It becomes twice as wide, with unchanged peak intensity, which depends only on the source.

questions.stem: A double slit has slits of width b = 0.10 mm whose centres are d = 0.30 mm apart. It is illuminated normally with monochromatic light. How many bright interference fringes lie within the central maximum of the single-slit diffraction envelope?
questions.explanation: Interference maxima are at sin θ = nλ/d and the first minima of the envelope at sin θ = λ/b. These coincide when n = d/b = 3, so the third-order fringes fall on the envelope minima and are missing. Inside the central maximum are the orders n = 0, ±1 and ±2: five fringes.

questions.stem: Monochromatic light is incident normally first on a double slit and then on a diffraction grating whose adjacent slits have the same separation d as the double slit. Every slit is equally illuminated. Compared with the double-slit fringes, how do the grating's principal maxima appear?

options.text: Farther apart than the fringes, because the grating has many more slits
At the same angles, but wider and dimmer, as the light is shared among more slits
Identical in position, width and brightness, because only d and λ matter
At the same angles as the double-slit fringes, but much sharper and brighter
